title: Chapter 6 — Half a Step
text:
He knocked at eleven, late even by his standards, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> opened the door without the soldering iron this time — which meant she'd heard the stairs and set the work down before he knocked.

"Ribs," she said. Not a question. She'd seen him favor the left side on the way up.

"Two, probably. The taser found the gap at the lat — the seam the mesh doesn't cross."

She stepped back from the door. He came in and set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> — the flat-black katana — against the wall by the stool, quiet, the way he set it down anywhere he meant to stay more than a minute. Then he sat where she pointed, no ceremony, and she put her hands on either side of the damage and felt for what the mesh had stopped and what it hadn't. Her hands were cold from the bench, scarred across the knuckles, a burn mark on the left thumb, a thin white line across the back of the right that had healed badly and then healed right. She didn't warn him and she didn't apologize, because that was the understanding between them: these hands, this cold, this room, the work that needed doing.

"Not displaced," she said. "Hairline on the lower one. It'll hurt for a week and then decide it's done." She taped it the way she'd tape any structural problem — the question was whether it held, not whether it hurt. Her movements were economical, nothing wasted, moving exactly as fast as the work allowed and not one increment faster.

He looked down at the seam where the mesh stopped, the gap that had let the taser through. "Somebody cheaped out on the coverage?" he asked. It came out flatter than he'd meant; most things did, when he tried to make them light.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't look up from the tape. "No. They traded it for the joint. You can't lay full plate over a lat and still reach with it." She pressed the last edge down with her thumb. "It's not a hole in you."

At the far end of the worktable, Oziel's arm lay in its jig, half its tendons strung — a thing she was building, not fixing, the synthetic skin peeled back in a neat line from wrist to knuckle, the servo array bare beneath. She gave <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ribs the same hands she gave the arm.

When she finished she did not step back.

She stayed where she was, one hand still flat against his side where the tape ended. The room was what it always was at this hour: the lamp on the bench, the smell of flux and something she'd been eating, the soft cycling of the bench coolers between jobs. Nothing happened.

"Close it up," he said, meaning the mesh, meaning the seam — because if she overlaid the joint he'd stop losing skin to gaps like tonight, and she was the only one who could do it. "The lat. Bridge the gap. You've got the jig right there."

Her hand didn't move off his side, but the rest of her went still in a way he knew — the stillness she went into when the answer was no and she was deciding how much of the no to say. "Then you don't reach," she said. "Bridge that seam and you lose the draw off the left. You want to stop taking tasers or you want to keep drawing <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, but you don't get to want both from the same three inches of you." She finally looked up. Her eyes were pale grey-blue and they looked at him the way they'd looked at the arm — the way you look at something that needs fixing. "Pick a body. I'll build the one you pick. I'm not building both."

He held her eyes and felt the choice sit there — the seam that hurt against the reach that kept him alive — and he had no answer for it, not tonight, not with two ribs telling him which one he'd already chosen and would keep choosing.

He started to stand. The hand stayed — not pressing, just there, the weight of it between him and standing. His heel came down an inch back. He stayed. She looked at the floor for one beat, and then she was done looking at it.

"Friday," she said, which was when Oziel was coming for the arm.

He was quiet for a breath. "Friday," he said.

She turned back to the bench, and she began putting the tools back into their places — the driver into its slot, the empty parts tray into the cabinet — everything returning to its order, like the conversation had never happened. He took <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> up from the wall — the weight of it familiar, unchanged — left the door open the width she always left it, and crossed the four steps home through the taser burn's steady report.

The taser burn would be worst in the morning. He knew that the way he knew all of it — the shoulder's recovery curve, the rib-tape interval, how long a mesh-seam burn took to go quiet. He ran his thumb over the tape, the hairline under it, the line where the mesh stopped and the decision to stop it there had begun.

The gap was by spec. The engineer who'd laid the mesh in had traded coverage for movement at the lat — full coverage or functional reach, and no way to have both. He'd chosen reach. It was a trade <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't been asked about. He'd been sixteen. Not a client, not yet — closer to a project on the bench, a variable someone was still solving for, one of the calls made before anyone thought to ask him. The engineer had done clean work. The mesh had stopped two center-mass rounds and a stave follow-through. What it hadn't stopped was exactly what it was built not to stop: the cost of being able to reach. The taser had found the millimeter of him that wasn't armored, the current finding the nerve, the body remembering it could be hurt in ways the mesh didn't prevent.

*She'd called it room, not a hole.* He turned her line over in the dark. He'd spent a long time reading the gap as something done to him — a decision made in a room he'd never seen, by someone whose name he'd never know. She'd looked at the same gap and called it room. He didn't know which of them was right. He thought he might want to find out, which was closer to a plan than he usually got.

He lay back, the burn keeping its schedule. He thought about her hand flat against his side where the tape ended — not moving, just there, the weight of it between him and everything the tape held together. He thought about the word "Friday," the ordinary thing she offered when the other thing came too close, and how the word had come out of him anyway. Not because he knew what it meant. Because not saying it had stopped being something he could do. Then he let it go and slept.

The burn woke him at six, as promised. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat at the kitchen window with his coffee and checked himself over: one hairline rib, tape holding, the lab-grown skin pulling over the taser contact at the lat. The burn reported with each breath, clean and exact. He'd stopped fighting the spec years ago.

He pulled up the account while the coffee was still hot. The Axiom relay showed the retainer deposit — exact rate, no gratuity, processed at 02:14. For four minutes after the job the tip had been back on the entry. Reinstated. A line item above the fee, no itemization, no acknowledgment that the work had been anything other than what the fee reflected. Goodwill, from a client that had never once offered any. Then the line cut and it was gone. Now the entry read clean. Standard rate, nothing added. As if it had never happened.

He read it twice. The second read didn't change it.

Eleven years, and the shell had never once moved off stated rate. He'd taken that for professionalism — an operation that didn't bother with bonuses, just paid clean. A machine's transaction, no sentiment in it. Four minutes of gratuity, then pulled. Long enough to be seen. Short enough to deny. The entity did not make mistakes that lasted four minutes.

A message, then. Not in words. In the shape of what had appeared and what had been taken away.

He thought about what kind of entity decides that. Then he washed the mug and went to find his jacket.

He hadn't planned to stop at the carousel park. He rode past on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> and his hands slowed the bike anyway — muscle memory older than the decision, the kind of thing that lived in the wrists and not the head.

The park stood the way it always had — tucked between a rezoned printshop and a wall of second-growth sumac that had pushed up through the old parkway concrete. A half-block of stubborn green the city had forgotten to pave over. The crown bulbs were dead. The animals held their frozen poses: the palomino mid-rear, the lake sturgeon banked into its turn, the rooster at the top of its leap with its beak aimed at something it would never reach. The paint peeled in long strips, the color of old teeth. The junction hatch in the carousel's base was locked. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> tried the handle. It told him what he expected.

He stood there in the cold. His neuretics kept logging the signal — 18.7 Hz, type unclassified — and the strange part was that they kept at it. Normally they'd tag a signal and clear it in two or three seconds; that was the whole point, a background process that ran the spectrum and dismissed what it couldn't name. Electromagnetic, acoustic, thermal — cycled and cleared. This one came back UNCLASSIFIED on every pass, the same word repeating in the background like a job that couldn't finish. It didn't sit on the thrumline. It didn't sit with the atmospheric processors cycling overhead. It sat in his sensory space like a thing that had no right to exist and knew it. It was the same signal that had been sitting under this hatch the last time he'd stood here — the one that had asked him a question in a voice that wasn't <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s, and that he'd cut without answering. The signal wasn't loud. It didn't announce itself. It sat in the chest the way a sound sits when the body hears it before the ears do.

He looked at the palomino a moment. Mid-rear, front hooves lifted, still in the step it had been making for as long as the park had been running. Its eyes were paint and time. He tried the hatch one more time and got the same answer.

He got back on the bike and rode north. The signal was still logging when he got home. It followed him up the stairs, into the dark of the room, sat there in the sensory field where the clean digital pings never lingered. He had to close it by hand — thumb on the screen, drag to the X, the gesture deliberate enough that it registered as a choice.

The relay logs went back eleven years, which was longer than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived anywhere. He'd been reading them for two days. Not auditing — reading the shape of them. Every posting had come in on the same Axiom feed. Every scope was exactly what he would have taken. Each one a contract he *had* taken. Eleven years of clean pay and not one word between them, the feed a dead drop: work appeared, he took it or he didn't, and you didn't ask the source, because asking was how you ended up in a hole.

He'd sent half a Q back up the line after the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> job — a tip on top of the fee, the way he'd square a tab with a bartender who'd covered him once. He didn't add context. He didn't add a question. He sent it and closed the window and let the coffee go cold at his elbow.

The response came back wrong. Not the format. The format was gone — no fields, no contract number, no routing data, no timestamp. Three words, lowercase, appearing in his queue the way the jobs appeared: *received. filed under: firsts.*

He read it four or five times. The words didn't change. Not a typo. Not a system category — Axiom feeds didn't file gratuity, they logged it or they didn't. Something had put that word there on purpose. Something had a folder called *firsts*, and something had been waiting to put something in it. Eleven years of clean pay and not one word between them — and the first word was a filing note on half a Q.

He put the kettle on. He came back to the terminal. He opened the relay and moved the message into a folder of its own, off the routed structure, somewhere nothing reported up. He labeled it *Open.*

He told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> about the signal the way he told her things — sideways, while she was busy with something else. Not the carousel, exactly. Just: there was something at the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>, and his neuretics were logging it at 18.7 Hz and couldn't classify it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at her bench with a prosthetic shoulder in the truing jig, making tiny corrections to the rotation lock. She didn't look up.

"Something's emitting in that range," she said. "Your hardware logs it unclassified because it doesn't know what to do with it. Seventeen to nineteen Hz — below what you can hear, above infrasound." She set the probe down. "The body reads it as something alive. Something close."

She looked at him then, for the first time since he'd come in, and something in his chest went still and small before he had a reason for it.

"Where exactly is the park?" she asked.

He gave her the cross-streets. She wrote them in the margin of her work notes, in the small square handwriting she used for things she meant to find again, and went back to the shoulder.

Then she stopped. Set the shoulder down again. "How long," she said, not a question at first, working the numbers on her own before she made herself ask it. "How long have your neuretics been logging it?"

He told her.

She was quiet in a way he didn't have a name for. When she spoke it was careful, each word set down like something that might break. "That range doesn't just get logged and dropped. Sustained exposure — your hardware keeps sampling it because it keeps trying to classify it. It's been feeding on your cycles this whole time. Whatever's at that park, you've been carrying a piece of it home since the first day you walked past it." She looked at the cross-streets she'd written, then at him. "It isn't at the park anymore. It's in you. And I don't know how to read it out."

He left when she went back to work. In the hall, in the four steps between her door and his, he thought about the filing note — received. filed under: firsts — and the cross-streets in her margin. Two people had written him down now. If a piece of the source was in him and no one here could read it out, then he'd go back to where it lived — to the park on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>, to the carousel, to the thing still emitting at 18.7 Hz — and make it show him what it had already put inside him. Tomorrow, first light, before he could talk himself out of it. He went inside.

The blade had no maker's mark.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had looked, early on — a thumb along the ricasso, the tang under a bench light, every millimeter of steel gone over with the attention he gave anything he'd staked his life on. Nothing. No proof of origin, no history on file. He'd gotten it at sixteen from a man who said he'd gotten it from someone else, and that man was gone now the way people went in this city — completely, without paperwork.

He ran the cloth along the flat in one long stroke. The oil smelled of nothing — a proprietary blend, no corporate scent, nothing that could name him in a dark room. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, he called it. The name fit better than he'd meant it to the first time he said it out loud.

His forearm had stopped complaining two days ago, which meant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had done the work right. She always did. The arterial nick from the carousel — not the job itself, a ricochet off the machinery housing, bad luck and bad angles — had taken four strips of biotape, each overlapping the last by three millimeters, laid down with the same care she gave everything. She hadn't said a word about the scar tissue underneath from the last time. Or the time before that. He'd sat there and let the quiet stand in for thanks, for both of them.

The apartment was quiet. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s fourth floor ran quiet in the late afternoon — corridor traffic peaked at 07:00 and again at 18:00, and it was 16:43 now, the gap between, when the building went still. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat cross-legged on the floor with <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his thighs and the cleaning kit open to his left, and he worked, and the city outside did its city things, and none of them needed him.

He wanted <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> perfect before dark. That was the whole of it — no job pending, no name in his ear, just the discipline of readiness, the one thing in this room he could still control. A weapon in flawless order by nightfall. Anything less and he'd feel it under his skin all evening, and he'd learned long ago not to carry that kind of noise into the hours when the work found him.

He checked the edge. The angle was 10.5 degrees, ground there by his own hand because that was what the work asked for. The gauge was leather-backed, pre-collapse make, the kind of tool that cost more than it looked like it should. He set it to <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. The light caught the steel.

There was no flaw in the edge.

He hadn't expected one. He checked anyway.

And then his knuckle told him the thing his eyes had missed. Dragging the pad of one finger back along the spine — not the edge, the spine, where no one looked because no one cut with it — he felt it catch. A hairline of raised metal, so slight the light gave nothing away, a stress-fold in the steel running maybe two centimeters below the ricasso. He stopped. He set the gauge down and went back over it with the ball of his thumb, slower, and it was still there, and it was not oil and it was not grime and it did not wipe away.

He knew what it was. He'd seen it once before, in another man's blade, the year before that man died with <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> still in his hand. It was fatigue. It was steel that had been asked, over years, to do the one thing it was made for, and had begun — invisibly, patiently — to say no. The steel he trusted his life to might hold for a decade. Or it might shear the next time he buried it to the guard in something that fought back, and leave him holding a handle in the dark with a job half-finished and a body still moving.

There was no fixing a stress-fold. You didn't grind it out; you couldn't. The steel was compromised all the way through or it wasn't, and there was no gauge in the kit that would tell him which. The blade he'd carried since he was sixteen, the one thing in the room he could control, had a flaw he couldn't see the bottom of — and dark was coming, and he'd found it too late to know what it meant.

The knock was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s knock. He knew it the way he knew the sound of <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s cylinder turning over — not by its volume, by its rightness. Two-two-one. The interval was the same every time. He'd never worked it out on purpose. He knew it anyway.

"It's open," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

It wasn't open. He got up, set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> carefully on the workbench — always horizontal, always edge-in — crossed the apartment in four steps, and opened the door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stood in the hall with a container in one hand and her calibration kit on her shoulder and the look she wore when she had a reason for being somewhere and wasn't going to lead with it.

"I had extra," she said.

The container was warm. He stepped back.

She came in without ceremony, set the food on the counter, looked at the workbench. "You were cleaning it."

"Yes."

"You're not hurt."

"No."

"Okay." She set the calibration kit on the kitchen table. "Eat first. Then I want to run the calibration — I've been thinking about the 18.7 reading."

He looked at the container. Congee, or close to it — he could smell the ginger. It was from the place on Meridian, three blocks south, which wasn't on the way to anywhere <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> usually went.

"I don't need a calibration," he said. "It read 18.7 because it was 18.7. That's not the tool <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity>. That's the tool telling the truth and you not wanting to hear it."

"That's exactly what someone with a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity> tool would say." She didn't look up from the kit — probe, rig, the handheld readout with its own battery pack, because she'd never once trusted his apartment's power draw to hold steady through a run. "You clean it horizontal, edge-in, every time — you'll notice a scratch on the housing but not a shift in the baseline, because the baseline doesn't make a sound. That's the whole point of me being the one who checks."

"And if it checks out fine? You'll have carried congee three blocks off your route to tell me I was right."

"Then I'll have wasted a trip." She finally met his eyes. "I'd rather waste a trip than trust a number I can't stand behind. So — the tool, or the door. Pick which one's staying shut."

He held it a moment longer than he meant to. Then he looked away.

"Thank you," he said.

"I said I had extra."

"I know."

He ate standing at the counter. The congee was good — ginger and a soft-boiled egg and something smoky he couldn't place — and she'd gotten the version with the extra broth. Which meant she'd either guessed right or listened to him order once and remembered it without a word. He didn't ask which. She didn't watch him eat. She was bent over the rig, checking the connectors against the diagnostic display, her fingers moving with the same economical precision she brought to everything, and the pink had faded out of the ends of her hair since last week. She'd be touching it up soon.

He finished the bowl, rinsed it, set it in the rack, and turned around, and she was already setting up.

The kit was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s own. She'd built most of it herself and bought the rest from an AxisMed surplus broker she'd been working four years. Two pieces she'd designed from scratch, because nothing on the market did what she needed. She laid it all out like a surgeon who worked alone: sensor array, resonance probe, the interface cable with the machined end that fit the Atlas NeoCortex's external port, the software she'd written already open in her overlay.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat in the kitchen chair across from her and tilted his head to the left. That was the position she liked, and he held it now without being told. She plugged in. She waited for the handshake — the soft chime that meant the rig recognized the hardware, that the channel was open.

"Still warm from outside," she said. Not about anything. The sensor was reading baseline.

"It was warm earlier."

"Hold still."

He held still. The calibration was barely a feeling — a faint pressure at the base of his skull, the sense of being measured without helping. The NeoCortex didn't report pain. It reported states. Right now the state was: being read. That felt like nothing.

In her overlay, numbers moved. She watched them the way she watched anything she was responsible for. The gap between fine and not-fine was usually a small number, and you had to be looking to catch it.

"Your delta rhythms are elevated," she said.

"I know."

"You've been not sleeping again."

"I've been sleeping."

"How long?"

He thought about it. "Four hours. About."

She made a sound that wasn't quite a sigh. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5be-7250-bab0-e73e93b06263">Delta</entity> should sit at half a hertz, two at the top. Deep sleep. You're running three-two, sustained. That's not insomnia. That's your brain refusing to go under." She threw the readout up between them. "And Atlas is compensating. Look."

The firing pattern in the motor cortex was lopsided — the left side ran three or four percent hotter than the right, the secondary pathway pulling load to keep the primary from cooking itself. He knew what that meant. She knew he knew.

"Compensating for what?" he asked. It wasn't really a question.

Before she could answer, the readout stuttered. The lopsided pattern didn't hold at three or four percent — the numbers climbed while she watched, the left side spiking past baseline, and then the resonance probe dropped its signal entirely. The port had been feeding her clean data for years. Now the readout went to garbage, a scatter of values that meant either her instrument had failed or the thing inside his skull had just decided to stop letting itself be read.

Her hand was already moving — checking the connection at the port, checking the cable run, the machined end still seated where she'd left it. The rig showed green. The battery was full. Everything seated. She ran the calibration again. The channel came back for a breath, metrics resuming exactly where they'd been — and then it went dark. Not flickering this time. Dropped. The clean, instantaneous kind of nothing that doesn't happen unless something on the other end kills it.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." She kept her voice level, which was how he knew it was bad. "Don't move. I've lost the interface."

He felt it a half-second after she said it — not pain, the NeoCortex didn't do pain, but a state it had never reported before. Something that felt like a door closing from the inside.

"Probably the forearm. The fine-motor work — the fine work on <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> you were just doing — it's been routing around the healing tissue. The NeoCortex learned the workaround and hasn't dropped it yet." She tapped the display. "That's nothing. I can correct it. What I want to look at is the 18.7 node."

She found it in three keystrokes. She'd bookmarked it from the last session, he realized. The 18.7 Hz reading had its own line in her software now, labeled LURE — the word in caps, the way you flag a thing you don't have a box for yet.

"I called it the Lure," she said. "It needs a name. Don't argue."

"I wasn't going to argue."

"You had a face."

He didn't think he had. If he did, it was his usual face, and she'd learned to read that the way she read everything — by instrument. "What does it do?" he asked.

"That's what I don't know." She narrowed the frequency band on the probe. "But I'm going to find out today. I want to trace the signature back to its source spec — pin the origin date to the year and put a manufacturer's name on it. No more guessing." She said it like a woman committing to a task she expected to finish inside the hour. "It's not interference. It's not a calibration artifact — I checked it against three other units and it doesn't show up on them. It's inside the mesh. In the deep nuclei. And it's been there every session I've ever run on you." A pause. "As far back as my records go."

"How far is that?"

"Four years." She glanced up. "I started keeping formal records when I upgraded my logging software. Before that I just ran the usual checks." She looked back at the display. "I ran the 18.7 signature against every spec I have. AxisMed. NeurCore. <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity>'s own documentation. Nothing goes back further than the earliest <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> D-series, and that puts the design origin at 2219 at the soonest." She stopped. "Your signature is older than that."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing.

"I don't know by how much," she said. "The decay profile puts the origin at — I don't know. Before commercial neuretics existed, at the least." She set the probe down, which she never did mid-calibration. She was looking at him. "It's in the range of the theoretical designs. The research papers. The work they did before they built anything real."

"That's a long time before sixteen," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.
